domain: Calibrating the physical clock: how fast atoms, tests and institutions can move

bottlenecks.name: Test, qualification and certification campaigns
bottlenecks.description: Environmental qualification (vibration, acoustic, shock, thermal vacuum, EMI), engine hot-fire campaigns, materials allowables, human rating and reliability demonstration. Evidence is generated in physical time and counted under standards (NASA-STD-7009, GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03, NASA-STD-6030) that do not yet say what AI-made analysis is worth.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~25-35% of a new system's critical path (integration and test ~25% plus qualification and reviews ~10%, illustrative, general); larger for crewed, nuclear and new-material programs
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Mixed. Solved in principle but expert-scarce: information-optimal test design, test-data reduction, model correlation, anomaly diagnosis; on-demand AI is the unlock (2027-28 in S2). Genuinely open: credible uncertainty quantification for rare events and model-form error, certified multiphysics numerics, and the institutional rule for counting analysis as evidence (NASA's own aircraft certification-by-analysis roadmap targets 2040-2050). No catalog family moves this directly.

bottlenecks.name: Fabrication, production ramp and supply chain
bottlenecks.description: Building engines, stages, satellites and test articles; ramping lines to rate; long-lead radiation-hardened parts, forgings, castings, solid motors and nuclear fuel; factory and tooling capex.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~20-30% of a typical critical path (fabrication and procurement ~25%, general); the binding gate on cadence for constellations and reusable fleets (Mach33 found New Glenn cadence gated by BE-4 and upper-stage production, not reuse)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Small. Generative design for manufacturability and additive-manufacturing process models help at the margin; AI-run factories and robotics matter only in S3. Rad-hard parts (12-24+ months), single-source suppliers, HALEU fuel and capex are physical.

bottlenecks.name: Flight-test iteration and reuse learning
bottlenecks.description: Hardware-rich build-fly-fix loops for new vehicles, mishap investigations, and the accumulation of flight cycles needed to extend reuse life and prove reliability.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: For new launch vehicles, roughly 40-60% of post-design schedule (Starship: 14 integrated flights in 41 months, 48-90 day loops in 2025, 63-66 days in 2026); for reuse economics, the gate that sets $/kg
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Moderate on the cognitive slice only: anomaly diagnosis and probabilistic life models (days instead of weeks). Zero on flight count: Falcon 9 needed 15 months from first landing to first reflight, and cohort lifetimes rose from 4.2 flights (2018 boosters) to 24 (2020 boosters) one flight at a time.

bottlenecks.name: Launch access, cadence and cost per kilogram
bottlenecks.description: Manifest slots, pad and range capacity, propellant logistics, and the price of mass to orbit, which together gate every mass-heavy downstream application.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~5-10% of schedule for most spacecraft (waiting for a slot), but the dominant economic gate for mass-heavy missions; Amazon Leo had reached about 11% of its FCC deployment milestone by Jan 2026
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Indirect only. Mach33 attributes the fall from $4,915/kg (expended Flight 14) to $656/kg (2027 base) 56% to reuse, 32% to payload and 12% to production learning. None is a mathematics problem; AI helps through faster anomaly closure and life models.

bottlenecks.name: Regulation and licensing
bottlenecks.description: FAA Part 450 launch and reentry licenses, NEPA environmental reviews for new sites and higher cadence, FCC and ITU spectrum, presidential-level approval for nuclear launches (NSPM-20), export control and human-rating reviews.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: ~5-15% of schedule overall; on the critical path for new vehicles, new sites and nuclear systems (environmental assessment 1-2 years, EIS 2-4 years, 180-day statutory license review after a complete application, general)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: High for preparation: flight-safety analyses and environmental documents are expert-scarce, solved-in-principle work. Real for regulator-side review capacity. Zero for statutory clocks, public comment, litigation and politics. Reform is already under way without AI (EO 14335, Aug 2025; FAA proposed rules Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026; FCC Part 100, Jul 2026).

bottlenecks.name: Capital and program funding
bottlenecks.description: Appropriations cycles and political decisions for government programs; equity and debt for commercial programs.
bottlenecks.share_of_effort: Sets the pace of government programs (Artemis II slipped 5-7 years; Mars Sample Return, Gateway and DRACO cancelled 2025-26) and of every non-SpaceX commercial program; not binding for SpaceX ($100.8B cash after its June 2026 IPO)
bottlenecks.ondemand_math_help: Cuts the engineering-labor share of development cost by roughly 15-30% under S2; does not change appropriations, politics or the hardware and facility share of cost.

nodes.title: Monthly flight testing of a fully reusable heavy launcher
nodes.description: A new fully reusable heavy launcher (Starship V3) flies at least 12 integrated flights in one calendar year, so flight data rather than analysis sets the pace of learning. This is the data generator that reuse, life-prediction and certification-by-analysis nodes downstream need.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starship has flown 14 integrated flights since Apr 2023: five in 2025 (intervals 48-90 days) and three in 2026 (Flight 12 May 22, Flight 13 Jul 24, Flight 14 Sep 28; 63-66 days apart) after a ~7-month gap for the V2-to-V3 change. Flight 14 was the first orbital flight and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The FAA authorized up to 25 Starbase launches a year in 2025 (general); LC-39A's first Starship launch is targeted for around year-end in the best case (Mach33).
nodes.why: Cadence is set by vehicle build and pad turnaround: about nine weeks per V3 loop with one active pad. A second Starbase pad, LC-39A and first reflights (expected early 2027) bring the interval to 3-4 weeks, giving 12 or more flights in 2027. AI barely changes this: Flight 12 went from Musk's 'about 6 weeks' (Jan 26 2026) to May 22, about 2.8 times the stated interval, because of hardware (a Starbase component failure in April, an engine-out in flight), not analysis.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Both V3 boosters flown so far were lost in landing burns, and a pad-damaging failure (as New Glenn suffered on May 28 2026) costs 3-12 months. Only five of the 25 authorized Starbase flights flew in 2025.
nodes.signpost: Starship flight count in 2027 (12 or more confirms); LC-39A debut by mid-2027; sustained intervals below 30 days.

nodes.title: Regulators review with AI tools
nodes.description: The FAA's Office of Commercial Space Transportation, the FCC, NASA safety boards and ESA reviewers use AI systems to re-run and check applicants' flight-safety analyses, environmental documents and safety cases, raising reviewer throughput 2-5x without changing the rules.
nodes.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed electronic license submissions and four burden-reducing Part 450 changes on Oct 5 2026 and a waiver of 13 statutory requirements on Jul 30 2026 (Federal Register). The FCC voted on a 'Licensing Assembly Line' replacing Part 25 with Part 100 on Jul 22 2026, aiming to cut satellite licensing from years to months. No agency has announced AI-assisted technical review of launch licenses (general).
nodes.why: Reviewer hours, not statute, set most of the time between a complete application and a decision (statutory limit 180 days, general). A reviewer who can re-run a debris-risk or overpressure analysis with an AI agent in hours instead of weeks moves the queue. Reform supplies the rules regardless of AI; AI capacity decides whether the reformed process is staffed at 300+ U.S. launches a year.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Agencies adopt slowly under procurement, FedRAMP, ITAR and liability constraints; much review time is interagency consultation, public comment and policy judgment that AI does not compress.
nodes.signpost: FAA or FCC announcing AI-assisted review tooling; published median license evaluation times below 120 days.

nodes.title: Tests chosen for information, not habit
nodes.description: AI designs development and qualification test campaigns with Bayesian optimal experimental design and sequential testing, choosing which tests, levels, sensors and replicates buy the most margin knowledge. Typical test matrices shrink 20-40% and re-tests fall.
nodes.status_oct2026: The methods exist (Bayesian experimental design, design of experiments, sequential probability-ratio tests) but are expert-scarce; space qualification follows enveloped levels and fixed matrices (GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03, general). NASA's certification-by-analysis UQ discussion group published calibration and validation challenge problems (Jul 2025).
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 139 is T3 but not load-bearing
nodes.why: A 'solved in principle, expert-scarce' problem: on-demand applied math puts an experimental-design specialist on every campaign. Development tests, which operators control, change first; formal qualification follows customer acceptance. If test campaigns are ~25-35% of the critical path and AI trims 20-40% of test count, schedule gains are ~5-10% before any certification credit. Family 139 (subpolynomial-query log-concave sampling, T3) concerns the posterior sampling these designs use, but practical posteriors are already sampled adequately; it changes theory, not campaigns.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Test count is driven by standards, customer requirements and workmanship screening, not information value; dropping a test that would have caught a workmanship error is a mission loss, so mission assurance will resist.
nodes.signpost: A NASA, Space Force or prime-contractor test plan citing information-optimal design to cut a qualification matrix.

nodes.title: Launch range and airspace scheduled by optimizer
nodes.description: Range (Eastern, Western, Starbase) and national-airspace scheduling for hundreds to thousands of launches and reentries a year is done by optimization tools that minimize hazard-area closures and conflicts, so range time stops being a cadence limit.
nodes.status_oct2026: U.S. orbital launches: 198 in 2025 and 140 by Oct 7 2026 (Wikipedia). Musk projects Starship launching 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026). Range and FAA airspace integration are coordinated largely by human schedulers (general).
nodes.premise_tier: n/a; 124 is T1 (conditional) and not load-bearing
nodes.why: Launch windows, hazard areas and range assets form a precedence-constrained scheduling problem that mixed-integer programming and heuristics already solve at today's scale; the gap is expert time and integration with FAA air-traffic systems. At 1,000+ flights a year from one coast it becomes a real constraint. Family 124 (polynomial-time scheduling on three identical machines, T1) is a theory result; its algorithm will not be what schedules ranges.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Range capacity is limited by physical assets, safety buffers and airline-disruption politics, not schedule optimization; at 2026-2028 cadence the range is not the binding gate.
nodes.signpost: FAA or Space Force announcing automated hazard-area and airspace scheduling; FAA-reported airspace delay minutes per launch falling.

nodes.title: A rulebook for trusting AI-made analysis
nodes.description: NASA-STD-7009, ECSS and Space Force test standards gain a defined way to count AI-generated analyses (with checked derivations, certified numerics and quantified model error) as verification evidence, with credibility levels that map to allowed test reductions.
nodes.status_oct2026: NASA-STD-7009 sets model credibility. NASA's certification-by-analysis guide (May 2021) and UQ position paper (Jan 2024) place wide aircraft adoption in 2040-2050 and call tool credibility the open challenge; the NASA-FAA CM4QC strategy (Mar 2026) targets computational qualification of process-intensive metals. No standard addresses AI-generated analysis (general).
nodes.why: Every test-substitution chain needs a rule saying what analysis evidence is worth. Standards bodies revise on 3-6 year cycles (general); S2's automated statement audits (2027) and verified numerics (2028) supply the evidence, so a first revision or NASA interim directive lands around 2029. Capped at Medium because it is regulator acceptance.
nodes.strongest_case_small: NASA's own roadmap puts certification by analysis at 2040-2050 for aircraft; standards follow experience and accidents, not capability; a single failure traced to AI analysis would freeze adoption.
nodes.signpost: A NASA-STD-7009 revision, NASA engineering directive or ECSS handbook naming AI-generated analysis; a CM4QC pilot granting qualification credit.

nodes.title: Root cause in days, not months
nodes.description: AI agents do the cognitive part of anomaly investigations (telemetry forensics, fault-tree pruning, physics re-simulation of candidate causes, corrective-action analysis), so return to flight is set by hardware fixes and verification tests rather than diagnosis.
nodes.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 returned to flight 5 days after the Feb 1 2026 upper-stage deorbit-burn anomaly, with the FAA accepting SpaceX's findings (33FG). Starship loops in 2025 stretched to 82-90 days after the Flight 8 and 9 losses. New Glenn was grounded after an Apr 2026 upper-stage failure, and a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion destroyed a vehicle and damaged its pad (Wikipedia). The FAA accepts operator-led investigations (general).
nodes.why: Diagnosis is cognitive and sits on the critical path: when the cause is clear, return to flight takes days (Falcon 9, Feb 2026); when it is ambiguous, weeks to months. Searching the cause space 5-10x faster cuts the diagnosis share (illustratively 30-60% of a 60-90 day investigation, general) to days; redesign, requalification tests and FAA acceptance remain. No new regulator acceptance is needed: the FAA reviews findings, not the tools used to reach them.
nodes.strongest_case_small: The slow investigations are slow because hardware must be redesigned, rebuilt and retested or a pad rebuilt (New Glenn), none of which AI compresses; SpaceX already closes clear anomalies in under a week.
nodes.signpost: An operator stating that AI tooling found a root cause; falling median time from mishap to FAA return-to-flight determination.

nodes.title: License analyses drafted and checked by AI
nodes.description: AI agents produce and cross-check the Part 450 flight-safety analysis (debris, far-field overpressure, toxic release, expected casualty), the ground-safety analysis and the NEPA environmental documents that operators submit, turning months of specialist effort into days.
nodes.status_oct2026: The FAA proposed (Oct 5 2026) consolidating flight-safety-analysis information requirements, dropping overpressure analysis for hypothetical public locations and simplifying containment; Advisory Circular 413.13-1A (Jul 2026) revised application guidance. Specialist consultancies and in-house teams prepare these analyses today (general).
nodes.why: These analyses use established methods (Monte Carlo debris dispersion, blast propagation, plume dispersion): expert-scarce, not research-hard. An AI running FAA-accepted methods needs no new acceptance; the FAA evaluates the outputs as it does today. Payoff: license modifications for new trajectories or cadence (for example New Glenn's 12-to-50-per-year review) are prepared in weeks.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Preparation is rarely the long pole for an experienced operator; the long poles are environmental consultations, public comment and interagency review.
nodes.signpost: An operator or consultancy publicly using AI-generated Part 450 analyses; shorter time from application to license modification.

nodes.title: Certification by analysis accepted for space hardware
nodes.description: NASA, Space Force and ESA mission-assurance practice grants formal test credit to validated analysis for derivative and similar hardware across structures, thermal, propulsion and avionics: protoflight instead of dedicated qualification units, reduced environmental levels, analysis-only delta qualification.
nodes.status_oct2026: Qualification by similarity and protoflight approaches exist for heritage hardware (general). NASA's aircraft certification-by-analysis roadmap targets 2040-2050; NASA-FAA CM4QC (Mar 2026) addresses additively manufactured metals; the structures domain places structural certification by analysis at 2030 in S2.
nodes.why: A dedicated qualification unit and campaign for a major subsystem costs months and often tens of millions of dollars (general). If AI-supplied credibility evidence lets derivative hardware skip qualification units, a typical derivative subsystem saves 6-12 months. First credit comes on derivatives and uncrewed missions where the customer owns the risk. Capped at Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Tests find workmanship and integration errors that analysis cannot; first-of-kind and crewed hardware will keep full programs; commercial operators already skip tests where they own the risk, so the gain is mainly on government programs.
nodes.signpost: A NASA or Space Force program formally dropping a planned qualification test on the strength of AI-produced analysis.

nodes.title: Test stands that run themselves
nodes.description: Engine stands, thermal-vacuum chambers, vibration tables and materials rigs run around the clock under AI control with adaptive test sequences and automatic data reduction, raising facility utilization from roughly 30-50% to 70% or more and cutting test-to-insight time from weeks to hours.
nodes.status_oct2026: Autonomous laboratories exist for materials chemistry (DOE Genesis Mission first awards Jul 2026, per the capability domain); large aerospace test facilities run human-scheduled campaigns (general). The scarcest facilities are arc jets, large thermal-vacuum chambers and nuclear test infrastructure (general).
nodes.why: Test facilities are the scarcest physical asset; doubling utilization is worth a second facility (2-4 years and tens to hundreds of millions of dollars to build, general). Adaptive sequencing (stop when the information is in) and instant data reduction compress campaign calendar time 20-40% without new physics.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Utilization is limited by article build, setup, safety and consumables (propellant, liquid nitrogen), not scheduling; thermal soaks and life tests run in physical time.
nodes.signpost: A propulsion or test-services company reporting autonomous around-the-clock test operations with utilization figures.

nodes.title: Nuclear launch safety cases in months
nodes.description: AI produces the reactor design analyses (neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, accident criticality) and the launch-accident nuclear safety analysis needed for presidential-level launch approval of a space fission reactor, cutting a multi-year analysis cycle to months.
nodes.status_oct2026: DRACO (nuclear thermal demo, Lockheed-BWXT contract Jul 2023 for a 2027 flight) was put on hold in Jan 2025 and cancelled in 2025, with DARPA citing falling launch costs. NASA unveiled Space Reactor-1 Freedom (over 20 kWe, nuclear-electric, two Mars flybys) in Mar 2026 for a Dec 2028 launch; its estimate reached $2.1B by Sep 2026 while Congress directed $10M to it in May 2026 (Wikipedia). Launch approval follows NSPM-20 (2019, general).
nodes.why: Nuclear safety analysis is labor-dominated and export-controlled; on-demand applied math inside controlled networks compresses it from years to months. Interagency review and presidential approval remain, so capped at Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Space reactor programs die of funding and politics (SP-100, Prometheus, DRACO), not analysis; HALEU fuel and fabrication bind.
nodes.signpost: A completed SR-1 Freedom safety analysis report and an FY2027 appropriation of several hundred million dollars.

nodes.title: Both Starship stages caught and reflown
nodes.description: A Starship V3 booster and ship are each recovered and flown again, the threshold that turns a $200-250M expendable stack into an amortizable fleet.
nodes.status_oct2026: Booster catches were demonstrated with V2 (2024-25); both V3 boosters flown so far failed in landing burns (Flights 12 and 13); Flight 14 expended both stages by plan. Musk: Flight 15 attempts the first ship catch with odds of 'at least 50 or 60 percent', and ship and booster refly 'at the end of this year or more likely early next' (Mach33, Sep 2026).
nodes.why: Reuse is a flight-test result. Falcon 9 took 15 months from first landing (Dec 2015) to first reflight (Mar 2017). AI shortens failure analysis between attempts but does not change the number of attempts needed.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Ship catch and heat-shield refurbishment are unproven; repeated failures could push ship reflight into 2028 (Mach33 bear case).
nodes.signpost: Flight 15 ship catch (about Dec 2026); first reflight of a caught booster and ship by mid-2027.

nodes.title: Reflight cleared by data, not teardown
nodes.description: Reusable stages are cleared for reflight from flight sensor data and a probabilistic life model (a digital twin) instead of detailed inspection, enabling booster turnaround under a week and ship turnaround under two weeks.
nodes.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 in 2025: 95% of launches on reused boosters, median booster on its 14th flight, 38-day median turnaround, 162 missions from 25 airframes; cohort lifetimes rose from 4.2 flights (2018 boosters) to 8.0 (2019) and 24 (2020) (Mach33). No Starship stage has reflown.
nodes.premise_tier: n/a (capability premise); 372 is T1 (conditional) and not load-bearing
nodes.why: Mach33's base case has flights per stack at 3.3 (2027), 4.8 (2028), 8.9 (2029) and 18 (2030). Model-based clearance that pulls this curve forward 6-12 months is worth roughly $1-2B on the 2028 Starlink manifest alone (Mach33's 2028 base-to-bull spread is $1.6B). Life data still accrue one flight at a time. Family 372 (Lame moduli uniquely determined from boundary data, smooth isotropic case, T1) supports identifiability for inverse inspection in principle; damaged composites and welds lie outside its hypotheses.
nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX scaled Falcon reuse through fleet-leader experience and inspection without formal twins; the limit is wear mechanisms (heat-shield tiles, engines) that only flights reveal.
nodes.signpost: Starship booster turnaround under 7 days; SpaceX disclosing sensor-based reflight clearance.

nodes.title: A U.S. fission reactor launched
nodes.description: The first U.S. space fission reactor since SNAP-10A (1965) is launched: Space Reactor-1 Freedom (nuclear-electric, over 20 kWe) or a Fission Surface Power / Lunar Reactor-1 unit.
nodes.status_oct2026: SR-1 Freedom targets Dec 2028 at a $2.1B estimate with $10M directed (Wikipedia); Fission Surface Power had three Phase 1 teams from 2022 (Lockheed Martin, Westinghouse, IX), a 2025 executive order prioritizing a lunar reactor, and a directive targeting launch readiness around 2030; NASA said in Mar 2026 that SR-1 data will inform Lunar Reactor-1 (Wikipedia).
nodes.why: HALEU fuel supply, reactor fabrication, zero-power criticality testing and integration take roughly 4-6 years from a funded start (general). SR-1 is underfunded for Dec 2028; a 2029-30 launch needs FY2027-28 appropriations. AI shortens analysis and the safety case, worth perhaps 6-12 months.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Every U.S. space reactor program since 1965 has been cancelled; cheap launch removed DRACO's rationale; the 2026 cancellations of Gateway and Mars Sample Return show how fast NASA priorities shift.
nodes.signpost: FY2027 appropriation for SR-1; DOE fuel delivery; a reactor criticality test.

nodes.title: Pads and propellant plants for hundreds of heavy flights
nodes.description: At least four Starship-capable pads operate (Starbase pads 1 and 2, LC-39A, SLC-37 or equivalent) with on-site or pipeline propellant supply, removing pad count and cryogen trucking as cadence limits.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starbase has two pads; LC-39A's Starship debut is targeted around year-end at best (Mach33). A Starbase methane pipeline ('Starpipe') targets Jan 2027 service; SpaceX filed for a 32.4-mile Florida gas pipeline (Oct 2026); a $100B Louisiana campus (five complexes, two pads each) plans construction from 2027 and first launches as soon as 2029. Merchant supply needs about 389 tanker deliveries per flight (Mach33).
nodes.why: Pad construction (2-4 years per heavy pad, general) and air-separation and liquefaction plants run on the physical clock. On-site propellant costs about $0.2M per flight against $1.7-2.7M merchant, and trucking becomes physically implausible above about 100 flights a year (106 deliveries a day) (Mach33). AI barely touches this; it bounds every high-cadence node.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Environmental reviews, litigation or a pad-destroying failure can delay a site by a year or more; SpaceX may run fewer pads harder.
nodes.signpost: LC-39A's first Starship launch; Starpipe in service; Florida Public Service Commission approval of the pipeline.

nodes.title: 100+ fully reusable heavy launches a year
nodes.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers fly 100 or more orbital missions in one calendar year.
nodes.status_oct2026: 2025: 330 orbital launches worldwide, 165 by Falcon 9 (no failures), 5 by Starship; 2026 to Oct 7: 237 launches, 113 by Falcon 9, 3 by Starship (Wikipedia). Mach33's reference case has about 90 Starship flights carrying 10,100 t of Starlink in 2028; Musk says 'more than once per hour' within 3-4 years (Jan 2026).
nodes.why: At Mach33's 2028 base of 4.8 flights per stack, 100 flights need about 21 new stacks (roughly $3B at $143M each) and four or more pads; at 2030's 18 flights per stack, about 6 stacks. Production, reuse reliability and propellant bind. In S2 and S3, AI-run factories and faster anomaly closure add 6-12 months; S1 reaches it about 2030 on SpaceX's own trajectory.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Falcon 9 took from 2010 to 2022 to exceed 60 launches a year (general); each Starship failure grounds the fleet for weeks to months.
nodes.signpost: Starship flights in 2027 and 2028 (30 or more in 2028 keeps S2 on track); disclosed flights per stack.

nodes.title: A second reusable heavy-lift fleet at scale
nodes.description: A non-SpaceX reusable medium or heavy launcher fleet (New Glenn, Neutron, Terran R, Long March 10B, Zhuque-3 or another) flies 20 or more missions with reflown boosters in one calendar year.
nodes.status_oct2026: New Glenn: announced 2016 for 2020, first flight Jan 16 2025, first booster landing Nov 13 2025, upper-stage failure Apr 19 2026, vehicle destroyed and pad damaged in a May 28 2026 static-fire explosion; the FAA's draft assessment would raise its cap from 12 to 50 a year (Sep 2026). Neutron: announced Mar 2021 for 2024-25, now NET Q4 2026. Terran R NET 2026. China recovered a Long March 10B booster after orbital flight on Jul 10 2026 (Wikipedia; 33FG).
nodes.why: Mach33 modeled 15-36 New Glenn launches over 2026-27 and found cadence gated by BE-4 and upper-stage production, not reuse; every competitor slipped 1-5 years against announced first flights. AI helps new entrants most (no legacy process) but cannot shorten engine qualification or pad rebuilds.
nodes.strongest_case_small: For U.S. customer prices only Western competition counts (export control, national-security rules); Chinese fleets do not lower U.S. prices.
nodes.signpost: New Glenn return to flight and reflown-booster count; Neutron's first flight; Chinese reusable cadence in 2027.

nodes.title: Launch licensing in weeks
nodes.description: Routine license modifications (new trajectory, cadence or payload class) clear in under 30 days, new vehicle operator licenses in under six months from a complete application, and FCC satellite approvals in months.
nodes.status_oct2026: EO 14335 (Aug 2025) ordered Part 450 reform and NEPA streamlining; FAA proposed rules on Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026 waive statutory requirements and cut analysis burdens; the FCC adopted a Part 100 'Licensing Assembly Line' (vote Jul 22 2026). The statutory review clock for a complete application is 180 days (general).
nodes.why: Reform supplies the rules (final rules plausibly 2027-28); AI on both sides supplies the capacity. Together they turn licensing from a 6-18 month item into weeks for incremental changes. Capped at Medium because it is regulator behavior.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Licensing was not the binding gate for SpaceX in 2025-26 (hardware was); NEPA litigation and environmental consultations remain; a public-safety incident would reverse reform.
nodes.signpost: FAA final rules on the 2026 proposals; published license evaluation times; Starship license modifications approved without delaying flights.

nodes.title: Crew and national-security missions on data-cleared reused hardware
nodes.description: NASA crew or mission-critical payloads, or Space Force national-security missions, fly on reflown Starship-class hardware whose reflight clearance rests largely on flight data and life models rather than teardown inspection.
nodes.status_oct2026: Falcon 9 analog: first booster reflight Mar 2017; NASA crew on a reused booster with Crew-2 in Apr 2021, about four years later (general). HLS was not human-rated as of Apr 2026; Artemis III became a low-Earth-orbit test (NET Jun 2027) and the first landing moved to Artemis IV in early 2028 (Wikipedia).
nodes.why: The four-year Falcon lag was mostly evidence accumulation and customer process. AI-produced credibility evidence (standard in S2 around 2029) can cut it to two or three years after the first Starship reflight (2027). Capped at Medium because it is customer certification.
nodes.strongest_case_small: NASA crew safety posture will require flight history, not models; HLS and national-security missions may use new vehicles anyway, making the question moot before 2031.
nodes.signpost: NASA or Space Force accepting a reflown Starship for a mission; a NASA certification baseline for Starship reuse.

nodes.title: Starship internal cost under $300 per kg
nodes.description: SpaceX's internal cost to put a kilogram in low orbit on Starship falls below $300/kg, against about $1,500/kg on an optimized Falcon 9 Starlink flight and about $4,915/kg on expended Flight 14.
nodes.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Keystone v1.3 (Sep 2026): Flight 14 about $4,915/kg ($250M stack, 52 t); base $656/kg in 2027 and about $300/kg in 2028 (bear about $560, bull $141); $13/kg by 2035. Falcon 9 optimized Starlink flight about $1,499/kg at a $25M internal cost.
nodes.why: Mach33 splits the 2026-27 decline (log basis) into reuse 56%, payload 32% and production learning 12%. None is a mathematics lever. This is the independent physical exponential in this tree: it would happen at the same pace with no AI math at all.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Internal cost matters only to SpaceX's own payloads (Starlink, orbital compute); outside customers see prices, not costs (see physclock-cheap-mass-customer).
nodes.signpost: Flights per stack in 2027; payload per flight approaching 100 t.

nodes.title: Customers buy orbit under $1,000 per kg
nodes.description: Third-party customers can routinely buy dedicated heavy-lift capacity below $1,000/kg, against a Falcon 9 dedicated median of about $5,300/kg and a rideshare floor of about $7,000/kg today.
nodes.status_oct2026: Mach33 Launch Unlock model (Aug 2026): Starship third-party ticket enters at about $3,975/kg in 2027 and fades toward cost with a 2033 midpoint (2030-36 range) as competitors reach cadence; Voyager's $90M Starlab contract implies about $900/kg for a 2028-29 launch. SpaceX flew 83% of 2025 mass to orbit.
nodes.why: Price follows competition, not cost: Falcon 9 list prices were stable for a decade, and Mach33 finds a one-year delay in credible competitor cadence delays external crossover by about a year. AI math reaches this node only by speeding competitors' engineering.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Anchor deals like Voyager's already price near $900/kg, so 'routine' is a soft threshold; the markets most sensitive to $/kg (Starlink, orbital compute) are SpaceX's own and see internal cost.
nodes.signpost: Published Starship rideshare or dedicated pricing; a second Starship-class customer contract below $1,500/kg.

nodes.title: Qualification cycles 30-50% shorter
nodes.description: Typical qualification of a new or derivative spacecraft or launch-vehicle subsystem falls from roughly 12-24 months to 8-14 months through fewer, better-chosen tests, analysis credit and autonomous facilities.
nodes.status_oct2026: Qualification remains test-driven; NASA-STD-6030 requires per-machine qualification for additive parts; new space materials take 10-20+ years to insert (Materials Genome Initiative: 20 or more years from discovery to market).
nodes.why: Composite: test count down 20-40% (optimal design), calendar time per test down 20-40% (autonomous stands), qualification units skipped for derivatives (analysis credit). The incompressible core is thermal-vacuum time constants, real-time life and creep tests (a 10,000-hour creep test takes about 14 months) and statistical replicates. Capped at Medium.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Organizations spend saved time on more testing; first-of-kind hardware keeps full programs; the cut lands mostly on derivatives.
nodes.signpost: GAO, ESA or company schedule data showing shorter qualification phases on programs started in 2028 or later.

nodes.title: Monthly build-fly-fix loops on new heavy vehicles
nodes.description: A new heavy-launch program sustains integrated flight tests at intervals of 30 days or less for six consecutive flights, with analysis and anomaly resolution no longer on the critical path.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starship V3 intervals were 63-66 days in 2026 and V2 intervals 48-90 days in 2025; Flight 12 slipped from Musk's 'about 6 weeks' (Jan 26 2026) to May 22, about 17 weeks.
nodes.why: Loop time is build plus test plus pad turnaround plus analysis. With two to four pads and reuse, build and turnaround fall under 30 days; AI removes most of the analysis share (illustratively 20-35% of a 60-day loop today, general). Learning rate then tracks physical throughput.
nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may reach 30-day intervals in 2027 on hardware alone; AI's contribution will be impossible to separate.
nodes.signpost: Six consecutive Starship flights at intervals of 30 days or less.

nodes.title: AI cuts development capital for new space hardware by 15-30%
nodes.description: Non-recurring development cost for new spacecraft and launch vehicles falls 15-30% under S2 as engineering labor for analysis, design, software and verification shrinks; hardware, test articles and facilities do not shrink.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starship program spend exceeded $15B by 2026, against roughly $400M for Falcon 9 development, and SpaceX directed all $3B of its 2025 space-segment R&D to Starship (Reuters via 33FG). SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after an $85.7B IPO in June 2026. Mach33 counts about $250M into orbital-compute hardware specialists since Jan 2025.
nodes.why: Engineering labor is roughly 40-60% of space development cost (general); halving its analysis, design and software content cuts program cost 15-30%. That matters most for capital-gated new entrants; for SpaceX capital is not binding through 2031.
nodes.strongest_case_small: Labor savings get spent on scope; hardware-rich programs like Starship spend mainly on hardware; government cost growth comes from requirements and funding instability.
nodes.signpost: Startup raises and program estimates citing AI-reduced engineering headcount; NASA cost-estimating relationships revised for AI.

nodes.title: A new reusable launcher from start to orbit in three years
nodes.description: A program started in 2027 or later reaches orbit with a reusable medium or heavy launcher within three years of program start.
nodes.status_oct2026: Historical: Falcon 9 about 5 years (2005-2010) and Electron about 5 years to orbit (2013-2018) (general); New Glenn announced 2016 for 2020 and flew Jan 2025; Neutron announced Mar 2021 and is NET Q4 2026; the BE-4 engine alone took from 2011 to first flight in Jan 2024 (Wikipedia).
nodes.why: Even with cognitive work nearly free, engine development (hot-fire campaigns, turbopump failures), pad construction (2-4 years) and flight-test learning set a floor of about 4-5 years. AI's best case removes about a year, and only programs started after AI adoption (2027-28 in S2) benefit.
nodes.strongest_case_small: This node is itself the small-effect case; the exception would be a derivative vehicle built around an existing engine.
nodes.signpost: A 2027-28 program reaching full-scale hot fire within 12 months and pad readiness within 24.

nodes.title: New satellite generations every year
nodes.description: Leading commercial constellation operators field a new satellite generation (new bus or payload, not only software) about every 12 months, against 18-36 months today.
nodes.status_oct2026: Starlink: v0.9 May 2019, v1.0 late 2019, v1.5 2021, v2 mini Feb 2023, v2 mini optimized (average satellite mass down from 623 kg to 575 kg, 96 Gbps), V3 (about 1 Tbps, about 2 t) first flown on Flight 13 (Jul 2026) and first orbited on Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026). V3's timing was gated by Starship, not the satellite. V2 mini production reached six a day by Mar 2023 (Wikipedia; Mach33).
nodes.why: Design, software and verification compress in S2; payload qualification, radiation testing, line retooling and the launcher bind. Faster generations raise capacity per kilogram (V3 carries about three times V2 mini's capacity per kilogram, Mach33).
nodes.strongest_case_small: Generation cadence is set by launcher steps and fleet economics (about five-year satellite life), not design speed; operators may prefer continuous incremental change.
nodes.signpost: A Starlink V3.x or V4 announcement within 18 months of V3; Amazon Leo's second-generation timeline.

scenario_contrast: Two clocks, and two exponentials. The physical exponential in space is already running and owes nothing to AI math: Starship reached orbit on Sep 28 2026, first reflights are expected in early 2027, and Mach33's base case takes SpaceX's internal cost from ~$4,915/kg (expended Flight 14) to ~$656/kg in 2027, ~$300/kg in 2028 and $13/kg by 2035, driven by reuse, payload and production learning. That curve, internal cost under $300/kg (2028) and pads and propellant plants for hundreds of flights (2028), is the same in S1, S2 and S3. S1 (Plateau): AI is a consulting-grade analyst from 2028; physical gates compress 0-5%; 100+ heavy flights a year arrive around 2030; institutional relaxers (credibility standards, analysis credit, reuse acceptance for crew and national-security missions) stay beyond 2031; programs run 10-20% shorter. S2 (Exponential, base case): cognitive work runs 5-10x faster from 2028, which collapses the cognitive slices that sit on the physical critical path: anomaly diagnosis (days instead of weeks), license analyses and agency review (weeks instead of months), test-campaign design (20-40% fewer tests). Experiment and fabrication gates compress only 1.1-1.3x, so tier 5-6 nodes move by 0-1 year, and institutional nodes move 1-2+ years earlier (credibility standard 2029, analysis credit and qualification compression 2030) but stay capped at Medium. Programs started in 2028 or later are ~30-40% shorter, consistent with capability-program-cycle-compression. S3 (Recursive): cognitive work is close to free from about 2029, and AI-run test stands and factories lift the physical multiplier to ~1.3-1.5x; heavy cadence reaches 100+ in 2028 and the customer price under $1,000/kg arrives about 2030, but flight cycles for reuse life, real-time endurance tests, statutory clocks, appropriations and orbital mechanics stay fixed. Across scenarios the ordering of the tree barely changes; what changes is how much of the remaining schedule is pure physics. Under S2 by 2029, more than ~80% of the critical path of a hardware-rich program is physical time.
key_insights: The launch-cost exponential is real, already under way, and independent of AI math. Mach33 attributes the 2026-27 Starship cost decline 56% to reuse, 32% to payload and 12% to production learning; AI moves internal cost by at most 0-1 year in any scenario. The client's 'exponential curve' for space through 2031 is mainly this physical one, and AI math rides on it rather than driving it.

Amdahl's law sets the ceiling. With roughly a third of a program's critical path cognitive and physical gates compressing 1.1-1.3x in S2, new programs run ~30-40% shorter, not 10x. The cognitive slices that matter most sit inside physical loops: mishap diagnosis, license analysis, test design and data reduction.

Announced schedules run long by 1.5-3x, and the slips are physical. Flight 12 took ~2.8 times Musk's 'six weeks'; New Glenn flew five years after its 2020 target; Neutron slipped from NET Jul 2025 to NET Q4 2026; Artemis II flew 5-7 years after its original window. The causes were hardware failures, pad damage and funding, which AI does not remove.

The highest-leverage relaxer of the physical clock is institutional, not physical: a rule for what AI-made analysis is worth (credibility standards, then certification by analysis). In S2 it lands around 2029-30, capped at Medium, while NASA's own aviation roadmap says 2040-2050. Every 'replace tests with analysis' node in other domains should sit downstream of physclock-credibility-evidence-standard.

Regulation is moving without AI: EO 14335 (Aug 2025), FAA proposed rules (Jul 30 and Oct 5 2026), the FCC's Part 100 (Jul 2026), and a draft assessment raising New Glenn's cap from 12 to 50 launches a year. AI adds preparation speed and reviewer capacity; statutory clocks (180 days), public comment and litigation stay fixed.

Reuse learning is bought one flight at a time. Falcon 9 cohort lifetimes went from 4.2 flights (2018) to 24 (2020); Mach33's Starship base goes from 3.3 flights per stack (2027) to 18 (2030). Data-driven reflight clearance can pull this forward 6-12 months (worth ~$1-2B on the 2028 Starlink manifest) but cannot replace flight cycles.

Capital is not binding for the leader and is binding for everyone else. SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after its $85.7B June 2026 IPO and has spent over $15B on Starship; new entrants raise in $0.1-1B rounds. A 15-30% AI cut in development labor cost matters far more to entrants than to SpaceX, but the customer price per kilogram still follows competitor cadence (Mach33: a one-year cadence delay moves external crossover about a year).

Lag ladder for other domains (S2): from design-complete to first flight, a smallsat or derivative payload takes 12-18 months, a new launch-vehicle subsystem 2-3 years, a new engine 4-6 years, a crewed system 5+ years, a space reactor 4-6 years from a funded start. No tier-5 or tier-6 node whose design depends on 2027-28 AI capability should fly before about 2029 (smallsat) or 2031+ (new engine or primary structure).

Government flagships remain politically clocked: Mars Sample Return ($7B and 2033, then $11B and 2040, then cancelled 2026), Gateway (cancelled Mar 2026), DRACO (cancelled 2025, with cheaper launch cited) and SR-1 Freedom ($2.1B estimate, $10M directed). No scenario compresses appropriations.

Method note: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted and the Firecrawl account was out of credits, so this research used direct page fetches (Wikipedia, NTRS, Federal Register, White House, NASA, MGI) and the 33FG/Mach33 research MCP; items marked (general) are unsourced background knowledge.
nil_effects: Launch cost per kilogram through 2031 follows reuse rate, payload and production learning; AI math moves it by 0-1 year at most.
Propellant logistics and cost: about 389 cryogen truck deliveries per Starship flight on merchant supply, and air-separation plants, pipelines and power, all built on the physical clock (Mach33).
Real-time endurance testing: creep (a 10,000-hour test is ~14 months), thermal-vacuum cycling, electric-thruster life tests of thousands of hours, and radiation dose tests at accelerator flux limits.

Reliability demonstration by test: with zero failures, showing 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence needs about 230 successful trials (n = ln(0.1)/ln(0.99)); only accepted model-based priors change this, which is a regulatory, not a mathematical, step.
Orbital mechanics: Mars departure windows every ~26 months (late 2026, early 2029, 2031) and 6-9 month transits; no compute shortens them.
Statutory and procedural clocks: the 180-day Part 450 review, NEPA comment periods and species consultations, ITU coordination milestones, and presidential nuclear launch approval.
Government appropriations and political decisions (Gateway, Mars Sample Return and DRACO cancellations; SR-1's $10M against a $2.1B estimate).
Pad, test-stand and large test-facility construction (2-4 years each) and scarce facilities such as arc jets and large thermal-vacuum chambers.
Human-rating risk posture: crewed flight tests and independent review boards are not shortened by better analysis.
Long-lead physical supply: radiation-hardened parts (12-24+ months), forgings and castings, solid rocket motors and HALEU nuclear fuel.
Failure statistics: a pad-destroying failure (New Glenn, May 28 2026) costs about a year regardless of how fast the root cause is found.
